# Quantifying multilateral contributions to surgical system development in low- and middle-income countries: an analysis of trends and opportunities

**Authors:** Nardos Getachew Bulfeta; Simon Fabry; Gabriella Yael Hyman; Geoffrey C Ibbotson; Kee B Park

**Affiliations:** 1Harvard Medical School Program in Global Surgery and Social Change, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2Department of Global Health and Social Medicine, Harvard Medical School Program in Global Surgery and Social Change, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3Department of Surgery, University of the Witwatersrand Johannesburg Faculty of Health Sciences, Johannesburg, Gauteng, South Africa | 4The Global Surgery Foundation, Geneva, Switzerland | 5Program in Global Surgery and Social Change, Harvard Medical School Department of Global Health and Social Medicine, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

Financial limitations have stalled the implementation of national surgical plans in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), which significantly rely on development assistance for their health expenditures. This paper describes the challenges and opportunities in accessing development assistance from multilateral organisations and quantifies the trends of their financial contributions to surgical systems in LMICs.

We analysed publicly available data from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation Financing Global Health database and Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development Creditor Reporting System. We analysed disbursements from multilateral organisations and reported values in the trends from 2014 to 2022, major contributing organisations, geographic variations and implementing partners.

Multilateral organisations mobilised $232 billion in development assistance for health from 2014 to 2022, with the highest amount in 2021, during major global crises. Only 0.4% ($901.5 million) of this was disbursed to finance surgical care. Approximately 84% was financed from multilateral development banks, primarily by the World Bank Group and the Inter-American Development Bank. Disbursements went mainly to system-strengthening projects on building infrastructure and blood supply systems. Orthopaedic surgery was the highest, while anaesthesia and critical care were the least funded surgical specialties. Recipient governments were the major implementing partners.

Despite a noticeable growth following the Lancet Commission on Global Surgery, surgical care remains underfunded at 0.4% of multilateral development assistance, compared with the 50% that goes to communicable diseases. This gap reflects the dominance of disease-specific global health initiatives in the multilateral financing landscape. Multilateral development banks are demonstrating increased capacity to address this shortfall in multilateral finance. They emerge as strategic partners to advance surgical systems strengthening in LMICs by offering flexible financing mechanisms and supporting recipient-led implementation.

Keywords: Global Health, Health systems, Surgery, Health policy, Universal Health Care

## WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

- Financial constraints have hindered the successful implementation of surgical plans in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). External aid contributes to a significant portion of LMICs’ health expenditure, and multilateral organisations are key partners in development assistance for health, having mobilised around $41.3 billion in 2021 alone.

## WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS

- This study quantifies the financial contribution from multilateral organisations to support surgical care in LMICs and analyses the various factors that determine the trends.

## HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

- As LMICs pursue Universal Health Coverage, aligning health financing policies with national surgical plans requires strategic partnerships with key stakeholders. This analysis examines opportunities from leading multilateral partners, providing actionable evidence to support country-led surgical systems initiatives.

## Introduction

Surgical care is a cross-cutting component over multiple health domains—including maternal and child health, trauma, cancer care, and communicable and non-communicable diseases. While surgically treatable conditions account for a third of the Global Burden of Diseases, approximately 9 out of 10 people in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) lack access to basic surgical care.1 This is reflected in the disproportionate burden of preventable morbidity and mortality in LMICs from surgically treatable conditions.1 Healthcare system integration in LMICs historically focused on strategies that reflect external donor priorities and accountability requirements.2 3 This process meant surgical systems operated in silos, resulting in inefficiencies and missed opportunities for prevention, early diagnosis and timely management of surgically treatable conditions.4

In a process that has gained momentum over the past 10 years, ministries of health in LMICs have developed strategic frameworks to improve and foster surgical care delivery through National Surgical Obstetric and Anesthesia Plans (NSOAPs). These efforts were fuelled by landmark publications and resolutions passed in 2015. The World Health Assembly resolution 68.155 on strengthening emergency and essential surgical care and anaesthesia recognises surgical care as a vital component of health systems and Universal Health Coverage. The Lancet Commission on Global Surgery6 defined the service gap and forwarded surgical indicators to monitor implementation efforts. The World Bank Group’s (WBG) third edition of Disease Control Priorities,7 and inclusion of surgical indicators into the World Development Indicators,8 highlighted the key role of surgical care in health system strengthening and economic development.

Despite the development of NSOAPs in over 25 countries, implementation has been stalled by the lack of sustainable funding.9 This challenge is particularly acute in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), where half the countries rely on external funding for more than a third of their annual health expenditures.10 This external financial support comes in the form of humanitarian aid—assistance in the event of crises or emergencies—and development aid, which supports long-term sustainable improvements in economic and social well-being.11 External funding has historically prioritised communicable diseases, where, according to the Global Health Expenditure Database, two-thirds of external health aid to LMICs between 2000 and 2019 focused solely on infectious diseases.12 In the era where the demand for surgical care is ever-growing and financial limitations significantly deter the successful implementation of national strategies, it is paramount to understand the global surgical care financing landscape.13

In 2021, multilateral organisations mobilised approximately 40% of total development assistance, underscoring their pivotal role in global development financing.14 While prior studies document multilaterals’ technical contributions to surgical systems strengthening, the scale of their financial support for surgical care remains unquantified. Therefore, this study addresses the question: “What has been the financial contribution from multilateral organisations to surgical systems in LMICs?”

## Methods

This paper comprises a semistructured literature review for thematic analysis and quantitative data analysis from various databases. ‘Surgery’ or ‘surgical care’ has been defined as “the delivery of surgery, obstetric, trauma, and anesthesia care, including support areas such as oxygen delivery, blood transfusion systems, infrastructure and technology”.15 Multilateral organisations are institutions that operate through the coordination of policies among multiple member states to achieve common interests. A distinctive feature of these organisations is that sovereign member states serve dual roles as both beneficiaries and governing shareholders, providing them with a voice and voting capacity in the organisation’s decision-making processes.16 17

As of 2024, more than 200 multilateral organisations exist but main organisations include entities within the United Nations Development System, multilateral development banks (MDBs) and vertical funds.18 The list of multilateral organisations explored in this manuscript is found in table 1.

*Table 1 List of multilateral institutions examined*

| Category | Description | Organisations included in quantitative and qualitative data analyses |
|---|---|---|
| UN system | Various funds and agencies in the United Nations System | UNICEF (United Nations Children's Fund), UNFPA (United Nations Population Fund), WHO (World Health Organization), PAHO (Pan American Health Organization) |
| EU institutions | European Union institutions | EU |
| Multilateral funds | Focused financial mechanisms or pooled funds targeting specific health sectors or causes | Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development (AFESD), Global Alliance for Vaccine Initiative (GAVI), Global Fund to Fight AIDS, TB and Malaria (GFATM), Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) Fund for International Development |
| Multilateral development banks (MDBs) | Regional development banks (RDBs) serving various geographic regions to support economic and social development | African Development Bank (AfDB), Asian Development Bank (ADB), Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA), Council of Europe Development Bank (CEDB), Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) |
| World Bank Group (WBG) | International Development Association (IDA), International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), International Finance Corporation (IFC) |  |

### Thematic analysis

We conducted a peer-reviewed literature search on PubMed and Google Scholar using keywords aligned with our working definition of surgical care (online supplemental appendix IA). We included papers from 2005 to 2024 to capture major developments and changes in the multilateral space (online supplemental appendix IB). We carried out abstract and full-text screening by two authors (SF, NGB) and bolstered the final pool using the snowballing method (reference screening) and a targeted search for white papers and grey literature from official multilateral organisation websites: WBG,19 African Development Bank (AfDB),20 Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB),21 Global Financing Facility (GFF)22 and the WHO.23 The sources searched for include organisational annual reports, country profiles, project appraisal documents and expert analysis on multilateral development assistance from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).24

Following final selection of relevant documents, NGB conducted inductive coding for paragraphs using Microsoft Word to identify and categorise content describing the structure, governance, capacity and unique characteristics of multilateral organisations. These codes were discussed between NGB and SF and refined into eight overarching themes. The resulting themes were used to summarise the findings and were elaborated further with illustrative examples which provided contextualised real-world evidence to enrich the interpretation.

### Quantitative data analysis

We retrieved quantitative data on disbursements from multilateral organisations from two publicly available databases: the International Health Metrics Evaluation’s Financing Global Health Database (IHME FGH)25 and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, Creditor Reporting System (OECD CRS);26 see also online supplemental file 1 for a description of the search process. These databases provide comprehensive data on official development assistance for health from various government donors, multilateral institutions and philanthropy. In addition, the databases provide recipient and implementation partner details, allowing for a thorough assessment of Development Assistance for Health (DAH) flow. Earmarked funds were not included in this analysis as they are identified as bilateral disbursements in the OECD database.27 All values are reported in 2022 US dollar value.

We used R Studio software V.24.4.2 for the data cleaning and analysis described in the online supplemental material.

The IHME FGH database25 was cleaned for duplicates, and the data for the dates from 2014 to 2022 were extracted to match the latest available OECD CRS data at the time of analysis. The database had <5% missing data (IHME uses various methodologies to impute missing data28). Multilateral organisations were filtered and grouped into ‘UN System’, ‘MDBs’ (RDBs and WBG), ‘Vertical Funds’ and ‘EU’ categories. Major aggregates of health focus areas, namely communicable diseases, non-communicable diseases (NCDs), reproductive and maternal health (RMH), neonatal and child health and sector-wide approaches (SWAps), were used to generate a smaller subset for comparison among health domains. Overall sum of disbursement to health versus the disaggregates by health sector already present in the dataset was reported to understand the trends of flow of DAH, major donors, channels, implementing partners, recipient pattern and key health focus areas.

The OECD CRS26 collects data from members of the Development Assistance Committee (DAC), non-DAC member states, multilateral organisations and philanthropy, allowing uniform comparison across organisations to address our main research question. We used the June 2024 version, which was the most up-to-date version of the dataset, which is updated twice a year.29 We took the values as the best available estimate of development assistance at the time of the study. The dataset had <5% missing observations and is unique in offering detailed project titles and project descriptions, which enables keyword search for identification of surgery-related projects. This methodology is adopted from IHME, which uses keyword searches in English and other languages to disaggregate projects into various categories.30

Data cleaning entailed the selection of DAC-health sector codes (120, 121, 122, 123 and 130). Extraction of surgical projects included a broad keyword search using search strings in English, French and Spanish (online supplemental appendix IIA, IIB, IIC). We used keywords to allocate the observations to surgical subspecialties and surgical system strengthening domains. The data extraction of surgery-related projects for the years 2014–2022 yielded 4895 observations, out of which 890 were on multilateral organisations. We examined the ‘Disbursement’ variable for analysis as it was the most relevant to our study. We identified 16 multilateral organisations that disbursed to surgical projects in our study period. We subset them as described for the FGH database. We supplemented the OECD database with additional databases for WBG (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD)/International Development Association (IDA), International Finance Corporation (IFC)) as described below. We assessed trends, key organisations, implementing partners and recipients, and compared findings to overall health funding from the IHME database to understand key differences in global health and global surgical care financing.

### World Bank Group disbursements

Targeted IBRD/IDA project information document search yielded 786 projects from 2014 to 202219 while similar review of the IFC website31 filtered for the same period retrieved 1943 projects including 107 in the health, education and life sciences sector across 21 countries and seven regions.

Project descriptions were screened with similar keywords applied to the CRS database, and disbursements to surgical care delivery component of the projects were manually extracted. US$ values were deflated to 2022 US$ constant and the IBRD/IDA sums were added to the total disbursements from the CRS database after removing the overlapping WBG disbursements in the CRS database. IFC disbursements were reported separately as they singularly pertain to the private sector. The selected project codes are outlined in the online supplemental material appendix II.

### Patient and public involvement statement

Patients or the public were not involved in the design, conduct, reporting or dissemination plans of our research.

## Results

### Thematic analysis

Our literature search yielded 304 peer-reviewed articles. After duplicate removal and title, abstract and full-text screening, 28 articles met our inclusion criteria. 13 additional articles were identified through reference screening of the selected papers, bringing the total number of articles included in our analysis to 41 (figure 1). The analysis drew on the thematic domains outlined in table 2 to characterise multilateral financing institutions, with particular attention to their governance structures and distinctive organisational features. The themes explored facilitators and constraints in the multilateral structure to examine how institutional design could support or limit investments in surgical systems. Common terms used in the manuscript are defined in table 3.

*Figure 1: Flow diagram of literature review for thematic analysis.*

*Table 2 Definition of terms*

| Commitment | A firm written obligation by a government or official agency, backed by the appropriation or availability of the necessary funds, to provide resources of a specified amount under specified financial terms and conditions and for specified purposes for the benefit of a recipient country or a multilateral agency.27 |
|---|---|
| Concessional | These are loans that are extended on softer terms than market loans, either through interest rates below those available on the market or by longer grace periods, or a combination of these.18 |
| Development assistance for health | Funds from and activities by donor governments, multilateral agencies and private agencies for promoting economic, social and political development in low-income and middle-income countries.13 |
| Disbursement | The placement of resources at the disposal of a recipient country or agency.27 |
| Earmarked funding | Funds in which the donor country has maintained control over its contributions to such an extent that the decisions regarding disposal of the funds are on balance taken at the donor’s discretion.27 |
| Grant | Transfers in cash or in kind for which no legal debt is incurred by the recipient.27 |
| Implementation channel | The entity that has implementing responsibility over the funds and is normally linked to the extending agency by a contract or other binding agreement, and is directly accountable to it.27 |
| Loans | Transfers in cash or in kind for which the recipient incurs legal debt (and the resulting claim is not intended to be traded).27 |
| Official development assistance | Official development assistance (ODA) is government aid that promotes and specifically targets the economic development and welfare of low- and middle-income countries.69 |
| Other official flows | Transactions by the official sector that do not meet the conditions for eligibility as ODA, either because they are not primarily aimed at development, or because they are not sufficiently concessional.27 |

*Table 3 Themes identified in qualitative analysis*

| Facilitators | Constraints |
|---|---|
| Wide operational capacityUse of innovative financing mechanismsExtensive technical expertiseStrategic alignments | Vulnerability to political influenceFragmentation and narrow funding baseFinancial pressure on recipient countriesEquity concerns |

### Facilitators

Multilateral organisations possess several advantages that account for their pivotal role in mobilising development assistance. They demonstrate adaptability in their structures and operations, which enhances their effectiveness in addressing evolving global health challenges.

#### Wide operational capacity

Multilateral organisations have an extensive international presence and specialised knowledge in specific sectors, such as healthcare and humanitarian aid, which enables them to effectively address complex global health challenges, including surgical care needs.14 They can bring together a diverse range of stakeholders—including governments, non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and private sector entities—to collaborate on global initiatives. This convening power facilitates coordinated efforts and policy development at the international level.32

Multilateral organisations also channel earmarked funds from governments and other donors to targeted areas and projects. Donors often prefer this approach as it reduces their administrative burdens while leveraging the expertise and widely established reach of the multilateral agency.32

#### Use of innovative financing mechanisms

Through strategic resource pooling from multiple donors, multilateral organisations amplify the impact of individual contributions. This collective approach generates significant multiplier effects, enhancing the scale and sustainability of development initiatives.14 Multilaterals offer a variety of financing mechanisms, including grants and concessional or non-concessional loans, tailored to the specific needs and capacities of recipient countries, to help governments and local or foreign private businesses expand investments. There has been a surge in funding schemes involving partnerships with for-profit organisations, venture capital and social impact bonds. Contrary to the UN system, organisations like the Global Alliance for Vaccine Initiative (GAVI) and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, TB and Malaria (GFATM) exemplify this trend by incorporating revenues from private partners, successfully reducing reliance on traditional voluntary contributions and shifting to more sustainable development finance.33

Multilaterals also increase their lending capacity through cooperation among themselves and by leveraging callable capital. Collaborative efforts enable them to undertake larger and more impactful projects than individual entities could achieve alone.34 For example, the European Investment Bank, in partnership with AfDB, Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) and the WHO, launched the Health Impact Investment Platform in 2024 to mobilise technical assistance, grants and investments to fund activities in improving primary healthcare in 15 countries.35 The Indonesian government recently secured $4 billion from four multilateral development banks—the WBG in collaboration with AIIB, ADB and IsDB.36 The project, running from 2024 to 2030, aims to improve health systems in Indonesia including surgical care delivery, addressing barriers to access by improving referral systems and reducing out-of-pocket expenditure for citizens. Out of this total, $275.4 million is allocated to purchase equipment that would enhance surgical and critical care in hospitals to tackle NCDs, reduce waitlists and improve services such as cancer detection and treatment.37

#### Extensive technical expertise

Beyond financial contributions, multilaterals give technical assistance, helping countries identify and implement structural reforms, strengthen their institutions and build resilience, enhancing the effectiveness of funded projects.34 By reducing administrative burdens, multilaterals ensure greater flexibility and responsiveness to the needs of recipient countries, facilitating a more efficient implementation of projects.38

Regional economic development organisations such as the African Union Development Agency (AUDA/NEPAD) and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) offer technical support and monitor country progress that aligns with their respective region’s agenda. AUDA/NEPAD, through the African Leadership Meeting Initiative’s commitment to steadily increasing domestic investment in health, has facilitated health financing conversations through regional health financing hubs and has shown its commitment to advancing surgical care in the region.39 40 APEC’s report on progress of efforts for cervical cancer elimination in the Asia-Pacific economies builds technical capacity and spotlights best practices from economies that promote partnerships between government, the private sector and civil society, as well as interventions that target vulnerable and at-risk populations.41

#### Strategic alignments

Multilaterals established vertical funds focusing on specific development domains which were not sufficiently addressed by traditional organisations. This targeted approach allows for easier monitoring and evaluation of outcomes, providing clear visibility of results that keep donors engaged and committed.14 The GFF has allocated funds to programmes that aim to improve comprehensive maternal care. For example, in Zambia, efforts focused on increasing the availability of fully functional emergency obstetric and newborn care facilities and improving blood supply, both critical for the surgical care provision.42

SURGfund, the only catalytic multilateral fund for surgical systems with donors consisting of government, philanthropy, private industry and finance sectors, pools and channels funds to frontline stakeholders to facilitate capacity building and the implementation of NSOAPs.43 This organisation is modelled on the success of GAVI and GFATM, replicating their strength in combining innovative financing mechanisms and focus on a target health domain to withstand fluctuations in global health priorities.

### Constraints

Despite the pivotal role multilateral organisations play in mobilising development finance, some of their inherent characteristics limit their capacity for engagement with LMICs.

#### Vulnerability to political influence

The increase in earmarked contributions alongside relatively stagnant core contributions from traditional donors has led to concerns about ‘pseudo-multilateralism’. Organisations like the WHO have been criticised for channelling earmarked funds to targeted projects, potentially bypassing the consensus-driven decision-making processes characteristic of true multilateralism.44

#### Fragmentation and narrow funding base

The rapid proliferation of multilateral entities over recent decades has led to increased fragmentation. This can pose risks to systemic coherence and accountability, resulting in overlapping initiatives and competition for resources among organisations.45 46 This fragmentation is also characterised by a narrow funding base, where a few donors provide the bulk of the funding, shape the agenda and priorities of the organisation, and result in financial vulnerability and over-reliance on resources from a handful of donor countries.45

#### Financial pressure on recipient countries

Co-financing policies implemented by some vertical funds require recipient governments to contribute a percentage of the planned grants, with the logic that governments will progressively assume increasing responsibility for programme costs. While intended to enhance sustainability, these policies can strain the fiscal capacities of low-income countries and potentially misalign with national health priorities.47 48

#### Equity concerns

Vertical funds, while effective in targeting specific diseases or health issues, may not directly address broader equity challenges or integrate with poverty-reduction strategies. This focus can inadvertently contribute to growing inequalities in access to health services.49 To mitigate this, multilateral funds such as GAVI, GFF and the GFATM collaborate to align health system strengthening funding, supporting components essential for surgical care enhancement. These include community engagement, data systems, supply chains and human resources for health.50

### Quantitative data analysis

#### Overview of multilateral development assistance

A total of $527.6 billion was disbursed as development assistance from 2014 to 2022. The role of multilateral organisations grew substantially in 2021 (online supplemental A appendix III figure), likely in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and conflicts, accounting for over $41 billion in disbursements and marking the highest DAH in a single year in history. This increase was mainly driven by a 1.35 times rise in development assistance from GAVI, GFATM and the WBG.25

From 2014 to 2022, multilateral organisations disbursed $229 billion, the UN system contributing $87.3 billion (38%), vertical funds $85.5 billion (37%) and MDBs, including WBG, $50 billion (21.4%). SSA was the highest recipient of region-specified funds, at $58.5 billion, 69% of which was sourced from vertical funds, and South Asia Seas (SAS) followed with $17.8 billion. WBG disbursed predominantly to SSA and SAS, where its concessional arm was prominent. Europe and Central Asia (ECA), Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) and East Asia and Pacific (EAP) majorly used the non-concessional arm, IBRD, whose disbursements in the last two regions were nearly matched by the respective regional development banks—Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and ADB.25

The USA was the largest government source for multilateral organisations, allocating $36.4 billion (16%) since 2014. More than two-thirds of this went to GFATM and GAVI, and 28% to the UN system, including the WHO, which received $5 billion (14%). From philanthropy organisations, the Gates Foundation channelled $6.9 billion through the WHO, and $8.9 billion through GAVI and GFATM. The WHO was the largest UN entity, disbursing 40% total UN funds and sourcing its funds from all types of donors. The non-concessional arm of the WBG (IBRD) sourced 99.9% of its funds from loan repayments, and the concessional arm, IDA, got nearly half its capital from loan repayments and the rest from governments and philanthropies.25

Approximately US$15.5 billion was designated as multilateral organisation administrative expenses, out of which WBG-IDA $2.7 billion, IBRD $2.1 billion and GFATM $2.7 billion accounted for 50%. These expenses more than tripled the yearly average of $1.6 billion to $5.1 billion in 2021. The WHO allocated its largest disbursement to SWAps and was the largest multilateral contributor to NCDs, followed by the non-concessional arm of WBG. UNFPA disbursed 61% of multilateral RMH disbursements and 20% of total development assistance for RMH25 (figure 2).

*Figure 2: Multilateral disbursements to various health domains in US$100 million, 2022 constant. NCD, non-communicable disease; NCH, neonatal and child health; RMH, reproductive and maternal health; TB, Tuberculosis.*

#### Multilateral funding to surgical systems: 2014–2022

Development assistance for surgical care totalled $3.4 billion from 2014 to 2022, just over 0.6% of the total development assistance for health disbursed in the same period. Bilateral aid accounted for $2.8 billion (82.3%), while multilateral organisations disbursed 15.5%, and philanthropy organisations gave the rest over the study period.26

Multilateral disbursements to surgical projects totalled $526.7 million. The trend after the landmark year 2015 showed a general rise to reach its zenith in 2019 at $124.7 million, followed by a 64% fall to $45 million in 2021. Pre-COVID and post-COVID (2019 vs 2022) amounts were comparable, as disbursements showed a recovery to $111.7 million in 202226 (online supplemental Appendix III).

Regional development banks disbursed more than 71% of this total at $376.7 million (figure 3), accounting for 11% of all development assistance for surgery. IDB had the highest disbursement with more than $238.3 million to LAC, ADB financed $62.4 million to EAP and SAS, and IsDB disbursed $52.6 million to Middle East and North Africa (MENA) and SSA. The European Union (EU), with $71.65 million; the UN System, with $50.8 million; and multilateral funds, with $22.1 million, account for the rest of the disbursements. AfDB did not have disbursements to surgical care delivery in our analysis.26

*Figure 3: Key actors in multilateral disbursements for health versus surgical care in 2022 constant US$. GAVI, Global Alliance for Vaccine Initiative; OPEC, Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries; RDBs, regional development banks; UNFPA, United Nations Population Fund; WBG, World Bank Group.*

As a function of the World Bank region, LAC received the highest multilateral disbursements with a total of $250 million, 95% of which was sourced from IDB and mainly went to projects on infrastructure and orthopaedics and trauma surgery. SSA received 36% of its $70 million funds from IsDB, and 32% from the EU, with contributions from UNICEF and OPEC Fund. The disbursements were directed to projects on infrastructure, blood supply, and obstetrics and gynaecology. It was also the only beneficiary of GFATM, which disbursed $5 million for surgical infrastructure in 2014 and 2015. ECA, supported by the EU and CEDB, focused on infrastructure and paediatric surgery with a total of $65.7 million. EAP, which received 84.6% of its total $44.4 million from ADB, focused on projects on infrastructure and blood supply systems. South Asia, 71% financed by ADB, with 15% from IDA from a total of $34.7 million, had projects on infrastructure, obstetrics and gynaecology, and orthopaedics and trauma surgery.26

Multilateral organisations directed 78% of disbursements towards surgical system strengthening projects, building infrastructure ($355 million), and blood supply systems ($45.4 million), both led by RDBs and the EU. Orthopaedics and trauma care with $76.7 million led by the UN System, paediatric surgery with $17.5 million led by CEDB and obstetrics and gynaecology $5.9 million led by the EU make up the top three funded single-specialty programmes. Anaesthesia and critical care, on the other hand, was the least funded specialty programme with $400 000.26

The IBRD/IDA disbursed a total of $374.81 million from 2014 to 2022 to surgical care delivery and system strengthening in Ukraine, India and El Salvador and multi-country implementation in Africa. Project details included strengthening management of NCDs and injuries, improving outpatient-based procedures and day surgeries, improving the prevention, early detection and treatment of cervical cancer, to strengthen capacity for collecting, analysing and sharing data on cancers through cancer registries, and to improve cancer management (online supplemental appendix III).19

This brings the total sum of multilateral disbursement to $901.5 million amounting to 0.4% of total multilateral DAH. During the study period, RDBs contributed 2.5% of their total health allocation to surgical care. The WBG disbursed 1% of funds to surgical care, while the EU allocated 0.13%. The UN and vertical funds allocated approximately 0.06% and 0.02% of their disbursements to surgical care, respectively.26

#### Implementation channels and flow types

Flow types are the types of finances provided by development institutions. The UN, EU, GFATM and Arab Fund disbursed 100% of their funds as grants to recipients. WBG, ADB and Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa provided only loans. IDB, OPEC Fund, CEDB and ISDB provided versatile finances, disbursing in the form of grants, loans or other official flows.26

Multilateral organisations used various implementation channels (online supplemental appendix III). The EU used multilateral organisations in 53% of disbursements, recipient governments in 14% and NGOs (either donor-based/international) for 10% of disbursements. The UN used only multilateral organisations for implementation. Approximately 83% of disbursements from RDBs and 100% from WBG and GFATM were implemented through recipient governments. IsDB disbursed $2.7 million in grants to the private sector in recipient countries. AFESD disbursed in the form of grants and loans to recipient governments and the public sector in the recipient government.26

#### Multilateral organisations and the private sector in low- and middle-income countries

The private sector is a key stakeholder in LMICs in terms of service delivery, medical innovation and financial capital.51 The evaluation of investments from the IFC therefore offers multilateral perspectives for the private sector in LMICs.

In our analysis, we found 26 investment projects from IFC for a total of $1.64 billion to surgical care. Half of these projects were in LMICs amounting to $369.7 million (22.5%) (online supplemental appendix III table ii). The Philippines secured $107 million for infrastructure. India secured $81.3 million for service delivery and health information systems. Companies in MENA secured 37.4% of the investments with projects in Morocco and Egypt securing $80 million service delivery, and those in Pakistan securing investments approximating $47.57 million for surgical infrastructure, service delivery and workforce training. SSA secured $25.4 million (6.8%). When summarised, the system strengthening projects consisted of building facilities for surgical care delivery, expanding workforce training, surgical equipment, and consumables, pharmaceuticals, and diagnostics. Surgical care delivery emphasised ambulatory (day) surgeries, oncologic surgical care, ophthalmology surgery, and orthopaedic surgical services. Around 63% of the investments were in the form of loans; 35% were equity with over $80 million in local currency including a concessional loan structured as blended finance.31

## Discussion

### The trends

Financial contributions from multilateral organisations to surgical care totalled $901.5 million, only 0.4% of total multilateral development assistance for health from 2014 to 2022.26 Changes in global health priorities, such as pandemics and conflicts, influence development assistance,52 and our analysis showed disbursements to surgical care in 2021 dropped by 64% from 2019 values, despite multilateral disbursements doubling to $41 billion in the same time period.14 The year marking the highest multilateral disbursement was also the year with one of the lowest disbursements for surgical projects. This reveals a significant funding imbalance across health domains, potentially driven by the unmatched influence of disease-specific global health initiatives that dominate the multilateral financing architecture.

Disbursements to surgical care went mostly to building surgical infrastructure and blood delivery systems, which parallel the critical infrastructure limitation in LMICs.53 One explanation for this heavy funding focus is that development banks have established expertise in infrastructure development and financing across multiple sectors and therefore more readily finance infrastructure projects in health as well.54 55 Another explanation is that investments in infrastructure offer an easily trackable and measurable outcome compared with investments in service delivery or workforce which have more compound measurement metrics.56 Training human resources in health faces well-documented challenges including high retention failures and delayed impact.57 This misalignment with the banks’ standard metrics could explain tendencies to favour investments in infrastructure projects. National surgical plans may have the potential to counteract this by establishing strategic priorities, robust monitoring and evaluation frameworks, and tangible timelines with measurable outcomes—thereby attracting sustainable finance.9

Despite anaesthesia and critical care being fundamental pillars of any successful surgical system, these essential services remain alarmingly underfunded, receiving less than 0.1% of total surgical system investments.26 When this chronic underinvestment is compounded by the critically low workforce density of anaesthesiologists in LMICs—ranging from just 0.02 to 0.4 providers per 100 000 population6—it demands urgent re-evaluation of investment priorities across surgical systems strengthening initiatives worldwide. Investments will need to be made to address the specialised workforce shortages in LMICs, as it is difficult to improve surgical care provision with less than 10% of the WHO-recommended workforce density.58

### The actors

While vertical funds and the UN were the largest multilateral organisations that contributed to health, disbursement to surgical projects was heavily carried by MDBs, including the WBG. This is visualised in the difference in disbursement to surgical care compared with all health, which ranged from 2.5% to 0.06% across the various multilateral organisations.26 We observe the effect this has on the regional trends of disbursements, where SSA received a major share of the region-specified multilateral support for overall health, while EAP and LAC took the surgical care counterpart. This reflects our thematic analysis findings, which identified equity concerns observed in the vertical multilateral system, that can inadvertently contribute to growing inequalities in access to health services, not only through discordant financial support but also through creating competing impacts on domestic investment priorities.49

The overall trend in financing surgical care and the susceptibility of development assistance to donor priorities has emphasised the need for a domain-based funding that can withstand sudden changes in global health priorities. The establishment of SURGfund,59 modelled on impactful multilateral global health initiatives such as GFATM and GAVI, may be able to replicate their success in ensuring sustainable financing for surgical care. However, given the cross-cutting nature of surgical care, such a design would theoretically not risk creating islands or engendering inequity, which vertical funds have been criticised for.33

Multilateral development banks demonstrated growing capacity to support surgical systems.26 Their expanding co-financing structures increase their financial and regional reach, reflecting their potential to support LMICs regardless of geography. MDBs primarily use recipient governments as the implementing partner, which points to government-led and government-executed programmes. While this supports recipient government agency and avoids the creation of parallel systems typical of vertical funds, it may not directly translate into successful implementation. Implementation efficiency gaps in government run systems persist and could be bridged through systemic engagement of civil society organisations and NGOs.60

Our analysis showed that the AfDB had the lowest engagement in financing surgical care in its region compared with other RDBs and their respective constituents. This has significant implications, as the majority of African countries require external support and have not yet managed to meet the 2001 Abuja Declaration to increase their government health budgeting to 15%.10

This reduced engagement in the region may be a reflection of how LMICs are reluctant to acquire more debt to invest in healthcare because the current form of deficit financing is more suitable for capital rather than recurrent expenditures.61 It may also be a result of the bank country strategies which did not give sufficient focus to the health sector.62 Weak public finances in Africa, and rising debt:GDP ratios exacerbated by the pandemic, also negatively affect African countries’ capacity to access more loans.54 In spite of these, the latest commitment from AfDB to disburse $6 billion in the 6 years from 2025 to 2030 in support of primary healthcare, including surgical care, and pharmaceutical manufacturing development,63 could be evidence of shifting outlook in the region and the opportunities available in development banks to address disparities in surgical care provision on the continent.

### The way forward

#### Aligning with the new global health era

We are witnessing the threat that a narrow funding base and shifting political climate pose to traditionally funded multilateral organisations such as the UN system. The withdrawal of the USA, the largest government donor to multilaterals, and the subsequent decrease in contributions from the UK and other major bilateral donors are uncharted territory.64 LMICs are ill-prepared to independently finance their systems, as demonstrated in their dependence on external support for a significant amount of their healthcare expenditure.10

As the WHO undergoes significant reform that addresses its weaknesses following recent changes in 2025,44 LMICs continue to tread the evolving global health financing landscape. Technical support from multilateral organisations remains as crucial as financial contributions. Using multilateral expertise to support the design of policies and frameworks, such as the NSOAPs, to achieve increased domestic health financing,40 mobilise private sector finance54 and monitor progress in surgical care provision41 would be fundamental to ensure that policies are feasible and can be realistically implemented in the target timeframe. In this regard, the implications for countries to maximise on multilateral support may include the following:

#### Identifying key partners

Sustainable financing requires identifying the right partners who align with LMICs’ surgical systems agenda.

- Multilateral development banks align with LMICs’ transition from aid dependency towards strategic partnerships that prioritise national health system goals. Their programme-based financing and direct use of recipient governments as implementation partners28 foster autonomy. Their versatile financing mechanisms to increase their lending capacity, use of innovative financing, concessionality and multibank co-financing65 provide a rich area for LMICs to finance surgical care. Indonesia’s co-financed Health System Strengthening Project is evidence of this capacity and can be a learning model for other countries.37

- The IHME Financing Global Health 2025 report shows that regional development banks were one of two organisations—the other being the Gates Foundation—which had positive growth in disbursements in 2025,66 making them a sustainable partner amidst shifting health financing landscape.

- Although financial data are not yet robust for SURGfund, early reports also show positive outcomes from a scale-up of locally driven projects. Strategic designing of programmes geared towards addressing surgical care disparities with coordinated government support attracts financing from multiple sources, as demonstrated in the Makueni County Project.59

- Private sector engagement from MDBs, particularly IFC, which offers local currency financing and innovative instruments such as blended finance, is an opportunity for the private sector to engage in surgical system strengthening.31 In times of economic uncertainty and increased debt burden, LMICs are devising strategies to mobilise private sector capital to finance health systems.54 The private sector can take advantage of this unique access to IFC financing to support innovation and surgical service delivery expansion.

#### Establishing financing platforms

AUDA/NEPAD’s African Leadership Meeting(ALM)-driven regional health financing dialogues and the establishment of regional health financing hubs40 are strategic moves that can be potentially adopted to include surgical care financing. Such platforms allow countries to continually assess their financial partners and rapidly respond to changes to prevent the reversal of progress.39 Creation of a surgical financing task force that is responsible for maintaining partnerships, providing monitoring and evaluation on progress, and designing and implementing programmes, along with ministries of health and finance, would increase efficiency and reduce fragmentation in the implementation of surgical projects.39

#### Recognising agency

Innovative multilaterals thrive through partnership with donor governments, philanthropy, financial markets and private organisations, which gives them the capacity to weather unprecedented changes.33 Taking lessons from global health initiatives to look ahead, a robust multilateral engagement will be highly dependent on country-driven initiatives that demonstrate feasibility and tangible return on investment. Countries should take the central role in financing small-scale programmes and generate evidence to engage result-driven external partners, such as philanthropy and global health initiatives.42

Research has demonstrated not only the cost of failing to invest in surgery but also the monetary67 and social gains of investing in surgical care. Surgical, Obstetric, and and Anaethesia (SOA) care is not a competitor for scarce resources; it is a synergistic partner in healthcare delivery that will allow countries to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals and Universal Health Care.68

## Limitations of the study

This study has limitations due to gaps in data tracking allocations to surgical care. Although our paper used the most comprehensive databases that best track and document DAH, allowing for uniform comparison, these databases are incomplete. Both the IHME and OECD lack full donor inclusion, for example, the IHME does not report on IsDB, the WBG disbursements are limited in OECD CRS and there is limited data on non-DAC emerging economies that do not report to the OECD. The provisional and estimated numbers in the OECD, which is updated at least twice a year, may vary at the end of the year once the full report has been finalised. The values in this study are therefore the best estimates available during the time of study. We supplemented these databases with quantitative analysis from multilateral organisation individual databases. ‘Surgery’ or ‘surgical care’ is not categorically reported in any of the databases used. We deliberately left out general terms—such as ‘operative’ and ‘operation’ to reduce false negative results and focused on DAC 3 Sector Codes 120–130 which may exclude some sectors that could potentially contain surgical projects (eg, 720, 730—Emergency response/disaster prevention). As the focus of this study is to quantify development assistance for health, we deemed this decision necessary.

## Conclusion

The pattern of multilateral contributions to surgical systems from 2014 to 2022 has shown that, despite a noticeable growth following the Lancet Commission on Global Surgery, surgical care remains underfunded at 0.4% of multilateral development assistance, compared with the 50% that goes to communicable diseases.25 However, multilateral organisations’ strong operational capacity, structural adaptability and innovative financing mechanisms make them a key player in supporting surgical care improvements globally.14 32

Within surgical systems itself, there exists a disproportionate gap in financing between various building blocks that outline potential perceived risks associated with investments in components such as workforce or service delivery. NSOAPs play a fundamental role in establishing transparency, accountability, and monitoring frameworks to mobilise development bank finance.9

Multilateral development banks have demonstrated their versatility to support surgical system strengthening through primarily recipient government-led programmes and private sector mobilisation.54 Given the substantial role of the private sector in healthcare provision in LMICs, strengthening of the private sector through multilaterals has the potential to create robust opportunities for public-private partnerships and support efforts to increase access to surgical care delivery.
